new_statements.rule_in_words: In words elicited in isolation, stress falls on the final syllable of the word in the Lebu' Vu' (Long Sela'an / Long Ikang) and Long San dialects; the author records no exceptions. Whether this final stress persists in connected speech is not addressed in the article (Blust 2013 suggests penultimate stress in phrasal context for languages of this type).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('invariably'). The underlying notebook (RB2-003-C, fetched sources) shows a handful of penultimate stress ticks ('ŋan 'sky?', 'uʔban, Long Ikang 'piʔən 'nine') among overwhelmingly final ticks.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms only (elicited wordlist forms from Blust's 1971 fieldwork at Long Sela'an, Long Ikang and Long San). Blust 2013 (sec. 4, Borneo) states as an areal generalisation that such Sarawak languages have final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context, and that stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo; Blust 2017 itself gives no phrasal data. The conflicting report 'regular penultimate stress but shifts to the final syllable if the penult is an open schwa syllable' (Smith 2020 AFLA 27 handout p.12; Kroeger & Smith 2024 snippet, both from Blust n.d.) is about Long Wat, a different Lowland Kenyah variety (Blust's Type B, closer to Sebop) that only shares the ISO code.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog long1406 'Western Lowland Kenyah' is scoped to Lebo' Vo' (Lebu' Vu', 'Long San Kenyah'): the Long San, Long Selaan and Long Ikang communities on the upper Baram (Smith 2017 p.14; Glottolog alt names; Blust 2017 'Lebu' Vu' Kenyah at Long Sela'an and Long Ikang, and the Long Tikan Kenyah at Long San'). The quoted statement (Blust 2017 fn. 11) is about exactly these three villages (Blust's Lowland Kenyah Type A). The ISO 639-3 code [ttw] was, however, defined on 'Long Wat' (CR 2007-247: one community on the Apoh, a Tutoh tributary, 'more closely related to Sebop and Penan'); Long Wat is Blust's Lowland Type B (Long Sela'an-Long Wat cognacy 61%, Long Wat-Sebop 75% in Blust 1974 via Kroeger 1998) and Smith 2015/2017 list it with Penan-Sebop, while Glottolog keeps 'Long Wat' only as a lexvo alternative name of long1406 and gives Sebop its own code sebo1238. The Long Wat stress rule (penultimate, shifting to final after an open schwa penult: Smith 2020 handout p.12; Kroeger & Smith 2024 snippet, both from Blust n.d.) therefore describes a variety that shares the ISO code but not the Glottolog referent, and it conflicts with the Lebo' Vo' report.

sources.locator: Appendix 'Phonetic transcriptions of the Long Sela'an voiced obstruents', footnote 11, p. 198 (PDF p. 22)
sources.note: Appendix (Long Sela'an phonetic transcriptions), fn. 11 p.198: 'Stress was invariably recorded as final in citation forms.' First-hand 1971 data from Long Sela'an, Long Ikang, Long San (Lebu' Vu' / Long Tikan Kenyah = Blust's Lowland Kenyah Type A). No other stress statement for Kenyah.

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2020. Tracing the path of constraint movement: the Austronesian binary-foot requirement and word-minimum phenomena. Handout, AFLA 27, National University of Singapore, August 2020, 52 pp.
sources.note: p.12: 'Kenyah (Long Wat dialect, Sarawak) has regular penultimate stress but shifts stress to the final syllable if the penultimate syllable is open with a schwa nucleus.' Examples *təlu > tələ́w 'three', *CəbuS > təbə́w 'sugarcane' vs *duSa > lúəh 'two', *bulu(-n) > búlun 'body hair'. No source cited on the slide (Long Wat data in Smith's other work = Blust n.d. fieldnotes). Concerns Long Wat (Apoh river; ISO reference variety of [ttw]; Blust's Lowland Type B, grouped with Sebop/Penan by Smith 2015/2017), not Lebo' Vo'.

sources.citation: Blust, Robert. 2013. The Austronesian languages (rev. ed.). Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics, sec. 4 (Borneo).
sources.note: Areal remark only: 'stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo... many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context. Final stress thus appears to serve as a marker of decontextualised lexical data.' Kenyah not named in that sentence.
